sections.heading: A table stores items, and each item needs only its primary key

plan.problem: A relational table fixes its columns before the first row, and a new kind of record needs a schema change. DynamoDB fixes only the key, so each item can carry its own attributes.
trace: **Create a table with a key.** When you create a table, [you must specify the primary key] (dynamodb-primary-key-required-at-create), and [no two items can have the same key] (dynamodb-primary-key-required-at-create).
**Choose one of two key shapes.** A primary key is a [single-attribute partition key or a composite partition-sort key] (dynamodb-faq-primary-key-two-forms).

**Leave the rest open.** [Other than the primary key attributes] (dynamodb-schemaless-except-primary-key), you [don't have to define any attributes] (dynamodb-schemaless-except-primary-key); the key is the [only required attribute for items in a table] (dynamodb-faq-primary-key-only-required-attribute).

**Store flat or nested data.** DynamoDB supports [both key-value and document data models] (dynamodb-key-value-and-document); [The document types are list and map] (dynamodb-document-types-list-map-nesting).

**Keep each item small.** An item can hold at most [400 KB] (dynamodb-item-size-max), attribute names included; a table has [no practical limit on a table's size] (dynamodb-table-size-no-practical-limit).
plan.table: What you define and what DynamoDB runs (columns: Part | You choose | DynamoDB does): Table | its name, primary key and one of [on-demand or provisioned capacity mode] (dynamodb-must-choose-capacity-mode) | the servers: you [don't need to provision any servers] (dynamodb-serverless-no-servers); Item | any attributes besides the key | stores and replicates it; Large file | a pointer in the item: [store the Amazon S3 object identifier] (dynamodb-large-items-store-in-s3) | nothing: the file lives in Amazon S3. One link per fact per cell; cells at most 15 words.
plan.why: Why so little schema? DynamoDB is built for access patterns you know in advance: you [design your schema specifically] (dynamodb-design-schema-for-access-patterns) so that the most common queries are [as fast and as inexpensive as possible] (dynamodb-design-schema-for-access-patterns).
plan.exam_signal: "key-value lookups, session state or shopping carts at any scale" points to DynamoDB, which AWS lists for [session stores or shopping carts] (dynamodb-decision-guide-key-value-session-store) with [single-digit millisecond performance at any scale] (dynamodb-decision-guide-key-value-session-store).
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence: DynamoDB [doesn't support a JOIN operator] (dynamodb-no-join-operator), and there are [no versions (major, minor, or patch)] (dynamodb-no-maintenance-windows) to upgrade. Reference only, no sentence: attribute data types ([number, string, binary, Boolean, and null] (dynamodb-data-type-categories); sets [must be of the same type] (dynamodb-set-types-same-type-elements) and [cannot be an empty set] (dynamodb-empty-set-not-allowed); DynamoDB [does not natively support] (dynamodb-no-native-date-type) a date and time type; nesting [up to 32 levels deep] (dynamodb-document-types-list-map-nesting)); key length limits (dynamodb-partition-key-length, dynamodb-sort-key-length); the BLOB advice of the FAQ (dynamodb-faq-blob-use-s3-pointers) is FAQ item 3.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: a table needs only a key, and each item can differ. The thing to watch is the size of one item.

sections.heading: A hash of the partition key picks the partition, so hot keys throttle

plan.problem: One server cannot hold every item of a large table, so DynamoDB splits each table into partitions. The partition key you choose decides how evenly the work is spread over them.
trace: **Hash the key.** DynamoDB feeds the partition key value into an [internal hash function] (dynamodb-partition-key-hash-decides-partition); the output [determines the partition] (dynamodb-partition-key-hash-decides-partition) that stores the item.

**Keep related items together.** Items with the [same partition key value] (dynamodb-composite-key-same-pk-sorted-together) are stored together, [in sorted order by sort key value] (dynamodb-composite-key-same-pk-sorted-together); this group is [called an item collection] (dynamodb-item-collection-range-retrieval).

**Copy each write into three zones.** A partition is storage [backed by solid state drives (SSDs)] (dynamodb-faq-partition-storage-ssd-multi-az), and DynamoDB synchronously replicates data across [three Availability Zones] (dynamodb-faq-sync-replication-three-azs).

**Give each partition a ceiling.** Every partition delivers at most [3,000 read units per second] (dynamodb-partition-max-throughput) and [1,000 write units per second] (dynamodb-partition-max-throughput).

**Throttle the hot key alone.** Traffic that one key concentrates creates ["hot" partitions that result in throttling] (dynamodb-hot-partitions-cause-throttling), with [throttling while other operations may remain underutilized] (dynamodb-hot-partitions-throttle-while-others-underutilized).
plan.table: Key design and result (columns: Partition key | Spread | Result): a key with a [small number of partition key values] (dynamodb-few-partition-keys-spread-writes), such as a status | most requests share a few values | hot partitions and throttling; a key with a [large number of distinct values] (dynamodb-uniform-distribution-distinct-keys), such as a customer ID | requests spread out | even use of capacity; a hot key plus a random suffix (write sharding) | writes [randomize the writes across the larger space] (dynamodb-write-sharding-random-suffix) | reads must [query the items for all the suffixes] (dynamodb-write-sharding-read-merge) and merge them. Never write that one partition key value always stays in one partition: without an LSI, DynamoDB can [automatically split your item collection] (dynamodb-item-collection-splits-without-lsi). One item is in one partition.
plan.why: Why throttle one partition and not the whole table? Each partition is its own unit of storage and throughput, and partition management is [handled entirely by DynamoDB] (dynamodb-partitions-managed-by-dynamodb), so the key is the lever you control.
plan.exam_signal: "throttling on a few keys while the table has spare capacity" points to a hot partition: choose a key with a [large number of distinct values] (dynamodb-uniform-distribution-distinct-keys), or add write sharding.
plan.diagram: dynamodb-hot-partition (after the table; caption and alt in diagrams)
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: adaptive and burst capacity (at most 70 words). Adaptive capacity is [enabled automatically for every DynamoDB table] (dynamodb-adaptive-capacity-automatic-no-cost) and [rebalances your partitions] (dynamodb-adaptive-capacity-isolates-hot-items) so that hot items [don't reside on the same partition] (dynamodb-adaptive-capacity-isolates-hot-items), as long as traffic stays under the [total provisioned capacity or the partition maximum capacity] (dynamodb-adaptive-capacity-hot-partitions-unthrottled). Burst capacity keeps [up to five minutes (300 seconds)] (dynamodb-burst-capacity-retention) of unused capacity; these details [might change in the future] (dynamodb-burst-capacity-may-change-not-guaranteed).
plan.body_extras: Reference only, no sentence: data on SSDs in multiple AZs (dynamodb-data-on-ssd-multi-az); the 99.99% SLA of one Region belongs to subsection 13 (dynamodb-three-az-replication-built-in); the throttling reason [`KeyRangeThroughputExceeded`] (dynamodb-throttling-key-range-hot-partitions); occasional throttling is normal (dynamodb-occasional-throttling-normal); the 20 KB worked example (dynamodb-partition-20kb-example).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: the partition key spreads the work over partitions. The thing to watch is one key that gets most of the traffic.
plan.stop_and_answer: A ticket app keeps the seats left for one concert in a single item, and every purchase updates that item. The table has far more write capacity than the purchase rate. When sales open, can purchases be throttled? Answer: yes; the item is stored in one partition, the one the hash [determines the partition] (dynamodb-partition-key-hash-decides-partition) for, and a partition delivers at most [1,000 write units per second] (dynamodb-partition-max-throughput); spare capacity elsewhere does not help. Spread the count over several items ([add a random number] (dynamodb-write-sharding-random-suffix)).

sections.heading: Read and write units depend on item size and read consistency

plan.problem: DynamoDB measures capacity in units, not in requests. A large item costs more units than a small one, and a fresher read costs more than a default read.
trace: **Count writes in 1 KB steps.** One write unit is one write for an item [up to 1 KB] (dynamodb-write-unit-1kb); a write rounds up to the [next 1 KB multiple] (dynamodb-write-rounding-1kb).

**Count reads in 4 KB steps.** A strongly consistent read of an item up to 4 KB needs [one read unit] (dynamodb-read-unit-strong-4kb); a read rounds up to the [next 4 KB multiple] (dynamodb-read-rounding-4kb).

**Read eventually by default.** [Eventually consistent is the default] (dynamodb-eventually-consistent-default) and needs [one-half read unit] (dynamodb-read-unit-eventual-4kb), but it [might not reflect the results] (dynamodb-eventually-consistent-may-lag) of a write that just finished.
**Ask for the latest data.** Set the [optional `ConsistentRead` parameter] (dynamodb-consistentread-parameter) to true to get the [most up-to-date data] (dynamodb-consistentread-parameter).
**Pay double for transactions.** A transactional read needs [two read units] (dynamodb-read-unit-transactional-4kb); a transactional write of 1 KB needs [2 write units] (dynamodb-write-unit-1kb).
plan.table: Units for one 10 KB item (columns: Request | Units): eventually consistent read | [1.5 RCUs] (dynamodb-pricing-provisioned-10kb-example); strongly consistent read | [3 RCUs] (dynamodb-pricing-provisioned-10kb-example); transactional read | [6 RCUs] (dynamodb-pricing-provisioned-10kb-example); standard write | [10 WCUs] (dynamodb-pricing-provisioned-10kb-write-example); transactional write | [20 WCUs] (dynamodb-pricing-provisioned-10kb-write-example). '10 KB' in the table title is an example value; the trace spells out RCU and WCU first.
plan.why: Why does a strong read cost twice as much? It consumes [twice as many database resources] (dynamodb-strong-read-twice-eventual) as an eventually consistent read.
plan.exam_signal: "must always read the most recent write" points to strongly consistent reads, which return the [most up-to-date data] (dynamodb-consistentread-parameter); "lowest read cost, stale data acceptable" points to the default eventually consistent reads, at [half the cost of strongly consistent reads] (dynamodb-eventually-consistent-half-cost).
plan.exam_trap_text: > **Exam trap:** A strong read does not work everywhere. Strongly consistent reads are [only supported on tables and local secondary indexes] (dynamodb-strong-reads-only-tables-and-lsi); a global secondary index or a stream returns eventually consistent data. <!-- trap: dynamodb-trap-gsi-strong-read -->
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence: on-demand counts the same sizes in request units: one RRU is [one strongly consistent read operation per second] (dynamodb-rru-definition) for an item up to 4 KB, and one WRU is [one write operation per second, for an item up to 1 KB] (dynamodb-wru-definition). Reference only: sizes are binary, [1 KB = 1024 bytes] (dynamodb-size-units-binary); list and map overhead (dynamodb-item-size-list-map-overhead).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: item size and consistency decide the units. The thing to watch is that a strong read costs twice as much.
plan.stop_and_answer: An item is 2 KB. How many write units does one write use, and how many read units does one strongly consistent read use? Answer: [2 write units] (dynamodb-write-2kb-example) for the write; the read size rounds up to the [next 4 KB multiple] (dynamodb-read-rounding-4kb), so the read needs [one read unit] (dynamodb-read-unit-strong-4kb). Do not write '2 KB' in the reveal: it is the prompt's example value, and the reveal is strict text.

sections.heading: On-demand mode bills each request and needs no capacity plan

plan.problem: A new product does not know its traffic yet. Capacity bought in advance is wasted at night and too small at the peak.
trace: **Choose a mode for each table.** When you create a table, you [must select] (dynamodb-must-choose-capacity-mode) either [on-demand or provisioned capacity mode] (dynamodb-must-choose-capacity-mode); [On-demand mode is the default] (dynamodb-on-demand-default-recommended).
**Set no numbers.** For on-demand tables you [don't need to specify] (dynamodb-on-demand-no-capacity-planning) the reads and writes that you expect.

**Pay per request.** On-demand is [billed per read or write request] (dynamodb-ondemand-billed-per-request-zero-traffic-free); an idle table [scales down to zero] (dynamodb-on-demand-scales-to-zero), and [there are no cold starts] (dynamodb-on-demand-scales-to-zero).

**Absorb peaks, up to a point.** On-demand [instantly accommodates up to double the previous peak] (dynamodb-on-demand-previous-peak-double); [throttling can occur] (dynamodb-on-demand-throttle-if-double-within-30-min) if you [exceed double your previous peak within 30 minutes] (dynamodb-on-demand-throttle-if-double-within-30-min).
**Keep the same service.** On-demand tables give the [same single-digit millisecond latency] (dynamodb-on-demand-same-latency-sla-security) and the same SLA as provisioned tables.
plan.table: On-demand settings (columns: Setting | Effect): nothing set | capacity follows the traffic; a maximum throughput | the table's [maximum read or write (or both) throughput] (dynamodb-on-demand-optional-max-throughput) caps it, to [keep table-level usage and costs bounded] (dynamodb-on-demand-optional-max-throughput); a higher warm throughput | the table [can instantaneously support] (dynamodb-warm-throughput-definition) more at once, and for pre-warming [you will be charged for those requests] (dynamodb-warm-throughput-default-free-prewarm-charged). Do not use the volatile fact dynamodb-ondemand-max-throughput-throttles-above-limit here.
plan.why: Why is on-demand the default? It removes capacity planning: you create a table [without worrying about capacity planning] (dynamodb-ondemand-fits-no-capacity-planning), and AWS calls it the [default and recommended throughput option] (dynamodb-on-demand-default-recommended) for most workloads.
plan.exam_signal: "unpredictable traffic", "a new application" or "pay only for what is used" points to on-demand: [On-demand capacity mode is the better choice] (dynamodb-ondemand-better-for-fluctuating-traffic) for traffic with spikes.
plan.exam_trap_text: > **Exam trap:** On-demand does not absorb every spike at once. It [instantly accommodates up to double the previous peak] (dynamodb-on-demand-previous-peak-double); before a launch far above any earlier peak, raise the warm throughput ([pre-warming] (dynamodb-warm-throughput-prewarm-for-peak-events)). <!-- trap: dynamodb-trap-on-demand-absorbs-any-spike -->
plan.startup_example: At most 30 words, numbers from uses_numbers only: 'Callvale's job writes swing from 2 calls a minute at night to 40 at peak. In on-demand mode, nobody sets capacity for either.' (story; the claim about on-demand is already linked in the trace).
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence: '[No account-level read and write throughput quotas] (dynamodb-no-account-quota-on-demand) apply to on-demand tables, but each table has a default quota of [40,000 read request units] (dynamodb-table-throughput-quota-on-demand).' Reference only, no sentence: the initial throughput of a new on-demand table (dynamodb-new-ondemand-table-4000-writes-12000-reads, volatile); the best-effort note on the maximum (dynamodb-ondemand-max-throughput-best-effort).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: on-demand charges per request and plans capacity for you. The thing to watch is a peak far above any earlier peak.
plan.stop_and_answer: A table in on-demand mode gets no traffic from Friday night to Monday morning. What does the weekend cost for throughput, and is the first request on Monday slow? Answer: nothing for throughput: on a table with no traffic [you are not charged for any throughput] (dynamodb-ondemand-billed-per-request-zero-traffic-free); and [there are no cold starts] (dynamodb-on-demand-scales-to-zero). Storage is still billed.

sections.heading: Provisioned mode bills the capacity you set, and auto scaling follows within minutes

plan.problem: A steady workload that runs at a high rate all day pays more per request than it needs to. Provisioned mode trades flexibility for a fixed, predictable bill.
trace: **Set reads and writes per second.** You [must specify the number of reads and writes] (dynamodb-provisioned-must-specify-reads-writes) per second that the application needs.
**Pay for what you set.** You pay for the [hourly read and write capacity you have provisioned] (dynamodb-provisioned-billing-basis), used or not.

**Throttle above the setting.** [Provisioned capacity throttling] (dynamodb-provisioned-throttling-when-exceeded) happens when the [consumption rate exceeds the read or write capacity] (dynamodb-provisioned-throttling-when-exceeded); the AWS SDKs [automatically retry requests that receive this exception] (dynamodb-sdk-retries-throttled-requests).

**Let auto scaling move the setting.** DynamoDB auto scaling uses the [AWS Application Auto Scaling service] (dynamodb-autoscaling-uses-application-auto-scaling) and a target utilization; AWS recommends [70%] (dynamodb-autoscaling-target-recommended).

**Expect minutes, not seconds.** Scaling starts after the target is breached for [two consecutive minutes] (dynamodb-autoscaling-two-consecutive-minutes), and it [takes several minutes to update the provisioned capacity] (dynamodb-autoscaling-update-takes-minutes-throttle).
plan.table: How often you can change it (columns: Change | Allowed): raise capacity | [as often as necessary] (dynamodb-capacity-increase-unlimited-frequency); lower capacity | [4 available decreases] (dynamodb-capacity-decreases-per-day) at the start of each day, up to [27 times] (dynamodb-capacity-decreases-per-day) in a full day; switch to on-demand | [up to four times in a 24-hour rolling window] (dynamodb-capacity-mode-switch-four-per-24h); switch back to provisioned | [at any time] (dynamodb-capacity-mode-switch-four-per-24h). The switch fact is volatile (changed 2025-08-12): it can stand in this table, never in a question key.
plan.why: Why choose it? For [steady workloads with predictable growth] (dynamodb-provisioned-fits-steady-forecastable), provisioned capacity gives [cost predictability] (dynamodb-provisioned-cost-predictability), and reserved capacity lowers the rate: [up to 54% off standard rates for a one-year term] (dynamodb-reserved-capacity-terms-and-discount).
plan.exam_signal: "steady, predictable traffic" with "MOST cost-effective" points to provisioned capacity with auto scaling, made for [consistent or predictable traffic] (dynamodb-faq-provisioned-for-predictable); add reserved capacity for a long, steady base.
plan.exam_trap_text: > **Exam trap:** Auto scaling does not prevent throttling in a sudden spike. [Throttling can occur regardless] (dynamodb-throttling-with-autoscaling-possible) of auto scaling, because it [does not respond instantly] (dynamodb-throttling-with-autoscaling-possible). <!-- trap: dynamodb-trap-auto-scaling-prevents-throttling -->
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: reserved capacity and the 35% rule (at most 70 words). Reserved capacity is bought in [100 WCUs or 100 RCUs] (dynamodb-reserved-capacity-increment) allocations; you [can't sell, cancel, or transfer] (dynamodb-reserved-capacity-no-transfer) it, and it is [not available for tables using the DynamoDB Standard-IA] (dynamodb-reserved-capacity-not-for-ia-on-demand) class [or on-demand capacity mode] (dynamodb-reserved-capacity-not-for-ia-on-demand). A rule of thumb: on-demand costs less when average utilization is [below 35%] (dynamodb-ondemand-cheaper-below-35-percent-utilization).
plan.body_extras: Reference only, no sentence unless words remain: the target range [between 20 and 90 percent] (dynamodb-autoscaling-target-range); target utilization as [the primary means of cost optimization] (dynamodb-provisioned-target-utilization-cost-lever); a new GSI on an existing table starts without auto scaling (dynamodb-autoscaling-new-gsi-not-enabled); scaling policies are [not automatically deleted with it] (dynamodb-autoscaling-not-deleted-with-table) when the table is deleted; the account quota of [80,000 read capacity units] (dynamodb-account-throughput-quota-provisioned); Database Savings Plans (dynamodb-faq-database-savings-plans-18-percent, volatile; chapter 41 owns discounts): no sentence.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: provisioned mode bills the capacity you set, used or not. The thing to watch is auto scaling, which reacts in minutes.
plan.stop_and_answer: A provisioned table with auto scaling serves a flash sale. Traffic jumps to five times the normal rate within ten seconds. What do clients see in the first minutes? Answer: throttled requests: auto scaling waits for [two consecutive minutes] (dynamodb-autoscaling-two-consecutive-minutes) and then [takes several minutes to update the provisioned capacity] (dynamodb-autoscaling-update-takes-minutes-throttle); the SDKs [automatically retry requests that receive this exception] (dynamodb-sdk-retries-throttled-requests). For spikes like this, on-demand mode fits better.

sections.heading: A Query reads one partition key, but a Scan reads every item

plan.problem: A read that walks through the whole table gets slower and costlier as the table grows. DynamoDB gives a cheap read for keys you know and an expensive one for everything else.
trace: **Name one partition key.** A Query must give the partition key and [a single value for that attribute] (dynamodb-query-partition-key-equality-sort-key-optional), [as an equality condition] (dynamodb-query-partition-key-equality-only).

**Narrow with the sort key.** You can [optionally provide a second condition] (dynamodb-query-optional-sort-key-condition) on the sort key with [`begins_with`, `between`, `>`, `<`] (dynamodb-query-sort-key-range-operators); items come back in [ascending order by sort key] (dynamodb-query-ascending-order-default).
**Scan reads everything.** A Scan [reads every item in a table] (dynamodb-scan-reads-every-item) or index, and [the `Scan` operation slows] (dynamodb-scan-slows-as-table-grows) as the table grows.

**Read page by page.** A Query or a Scan returns at most [1 MB per call] (dynamodb-query-result-1mb); you continue with `LastEvaluatedKey`, and you are done only when [`LastEvaluatedKey` is empty] (dynamodb-query-lastevaluatedkey-not-end).

**Filter after reading.** A filter expression is [applied after a `Scan` finishes] (dynamodb-scan-filter-same-read-capacity), so the Scan [consumes the same amount of read capacity] (dynamodb-scan-filter-same-read-capacity).
plan.table: What each read operation reads (columns: Operation | Reads | Use it for): GetItem | one item by its full key | one known item; Query | one item collection, or part of it | items that share a partition key; Scan | it [always scans the entire table or secondary index] (dynamodb-scan-less-efficient-than-query) | rare full reads and small tables.
plan.why: Why is a Query so narrow? A NoSQL table is [queried efficiently in a limited number of ways] (dynamodb-nosql-queries-efficient-in-limited-ways); outside them, [queries can be expensive and slow] (dynamodb-nosql-queries-efficient-in-limited-ways).
plan.exam_signal: "a Scan with a filter uses too much read capacity" points to a design in which the application can [use `Query` instead of `Scan`] (dynamodb-use-query-instead-of-scan), often through a secondary index.
plan.exam_trap_text: > **Exam trap:** A filter does not lower the bill of a Query either. A Query also [consumes the same amount of read capacity] (dynamodb-query-filter-same-read-capacity) with or without a filter expression. <!-- trap: dynamodb-trap-filter-saves-capacity -->
plan.try_it: dynamodb-t02 (Try it callout, one line, in this subsection: 'Compare a Query and a Scan with consumed capacity shown' in 3-do.md)
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: big scans without hurting the application (at most 70 words). A parallel scan is [much faster than a sequential one] (dynamodb-parallel-scan-faster-for-large-tables), but it can [consume all of your table's provisioned read capacity] (dynamodb-parallel-scan-heavy-demand). Lower the impact by [setting a smaller page size] (dynamodb-scan-reduce-page-size), or run scans on a table that is [not taking "mission-critical" traffic] (dynamodb-scan-isolate-from-critical-table). For a full copy, export to Amazon S3 (subsection 12).
plan.body_extras: Reference only, no sentence: a projection or filter does not change Scan capacity (dynamodb-read-capacity-by-items-read-not-returned); `Limit` applies [prior to filter expression evaluation] (dynamodb-scan-limit-before-filter); BatchGetItem and BatchWriteItem limits (dynamodb-batchget-limits, dynamodb-batchwrite-limits); PartiQL gives [SQL-compatible query access] (dynamodb-partiql-structured-semistructured-nested) but no joins (no fact says it adds none: no sentence about joins and PartiQL); expression limits (dynamodb-expression-max-length, dynamodb-expression-max-operators).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: a Query reads one key's items, and a Scan reads them all. The thing to watch is a filter, which hides items you still pay for.
plan.stop_and_answer: A table has the partition key `customer_id` and the sort key `order_date`. The application needs one customer's orders from March. Which operation, with which conditions? Answer: a Query with `customer_id` [as an equality condition] (dynamodb-query-partition-key-equality-only) and a `between` condition on `order_date`, one of the range operators [`begins_with`, `between`, `>`, `<`] (dynamodb-query-sort-key-range-operators); no Scan.

sections.heading: Secondary indexes give the same items a second key to query

plan.problem: A table answers fast only for its own key. A new question, such as 'all open orders' or 'one customer's orders by amount', needs another key.
trace: **Copy items under a new key.** You can [retrieve data from the index using a `Query`] (dynamodb-gsi-queried-like-a-table), and [DynamoDB maintains indexes automatically] (dynamodb-indexes-maintained-automatically) when items change.

**Global: any key, any time.** A GSI's [index key schema can be different] (dynamodb-gsi-key-schema-can-differ), it lets you [query over the entire table, across all partitions] (dynamodb-index-queries-span-table-gsi-vs-single-partition-lsi), and you can [add a new global secondary index] (dynamodb-index-online-operations-gsi-vs-lsi) to an existing table.

**Global copies lag.** GSIs are [updated asynchronously, using an eventually consistent model] (dynamodb-gsi-updated-asynchronously), and their queries [support eventual consistency only] (dynamodb-index-read-consistency-gsi-vs-lsi).

**Local: same partition key, another sort key.** An LSI has the [same partition key as the base table] (dynamodb-lsi-same-partition-key) and [a different sort key] (dynamodb-lsi-same-partition-key); it is [created when the table is created] (dynamodb-lsi-created-with-table) and allows [either eventually consistent or strongly consistent reads] (dynamodb-lsi-strongly-consistent-allowed).

**Project what you will read.** [global secondary index queries cannot fetch attributes] (dynamodb-gsi-query-cannot-fetch-from-table) from the table, so project them; the [`KEYS_ONLY` option] (dynamodb-projection-keys-only-smallest) gives the [smallest possible secondary index] (dynamodb-projection-keys-only-smallest).
plan.table: Capacity and size (columns: Index | Capacity | Size): GSI | [its own provisioned throughput capacity] (dynamodb-autoscaling-supports-gsi-own-capacity) | [no size restrictions for global secondary indexes] (dynamodb-index-lsi-size-limit-per-partition-key); LSI | it uses the table's: LSIs [consume capacity from the base table] (dynamodb-rightsize-lsi-uses-base-table-capacity) | each item collection [10 GB or less] (dynamodb-index-lsi-size-limit-per-partition-key). The GSI-or-LSI decision table is in 1-fast.md; this table adds capacity and size only.
plan.why: Why two kinds? An LSI keeps each item collection in one partition, which allows strong reads but caps the collection at [10 GB] (dynamodb-lsi-collection-one-partition); a GSI is [stored separately from the data] (dynamodb-gsi-data-stored-separately) of the table, so it grows freely but lags.
plan.exam_signal: "query on an attribute that is not the key" points to a GSI; DynamoDB queries nonkey attributes with [global secondary indexes and local secondary indexes] (dynamodb-faq-query-nonkey-via-gsi-lsi), and while a GSI is added, [the table continues to be available] (dynamodb-gsi-add-to-existing-table).
plan.exam_trap_text: > **Exam trap:** A table that already exists cannot get a new LSI. You [cannot add a local secondary index] (dynamodb-index-online-operations-gsi-vs-lsi) to an existing table; add a GSI instead. <!-- trap: dynamodb-trap-lsi-added-later -->
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: sparse indexes and back-pressure (at most 70 words). A GSI [only tracks data items] (dynamodb-gsi-only-items-with-key-attributes) whose [key attributes actually exist] (dynamodb-gsi-only-items-with-key-attributes), so an attribute that only open orders carry makes a sparse index; it is [faster and less expensive to query that index] (dynamodb-sparse-index-faster-cheaper-than-scan) than to scan. If a GSI lacks write capacity, DynamoDB [throttles writes to the base table] (dynamodb-gsi-back-pressure-definition).
plan.body_extras: Reference only, no sentence unless words remain: index limits [up to 20 global secondary indexes] and [up to 5 local secondary indexes] (dynamodb-index-limits-20-gsi-5-lsi) are in Numbers; a GSI's write capacity should be [equal or greater than the write capacity] (dynamodb-gsi-write-capacity-equal-or-greater) of the table; an LSI query can fetch unprojected attributes at a cost (dynamodb-lsi-query-fetches-unprojected-attributes); multi-attribute GSI keys (dynamodb-faq-gsi-primary-key-attributes, volatile): Changed recently only.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: an index gives your items a second key. The thing to watch is that a global index lags behind the table.
plan.stop_and_answer: An `orders` table has the partition key `order_id` and holds a year of data. Support staff need all orders of one email address, newest first. What do you add? Answer: a GSI with the partition key `email` and the sort key `order_date`, because its [index key schema can be different] (dynamodb-gsi-key-schema-can-differ); query it in descending order ([request descending order] (dynamodb-query-ascending-order-default)). An LSI cannot help: it keeps the table's partition key.

sections.heading: Conditional writes and transactions stop one write from overwriting another

plan.problem: Two workers read the same item, change it and write it back. Without a check, the second write silently erases the first one.
trace: **Overwrite by default.** `PutItem` and `DeleteItem` are [unconditional] (dynamodb-writes-unconditional-by-default): each one [overwrites an existing item] (dynamodb-writes-unconditional-by-default) that has the same key.

**Add a condition.** [A conditional write succeeds] (dynamodb-conditional-write-succeeds-only-if-condition) only if the item attributes [meet one or more expected conditions] (dynamodb-conditional-write-succeeds-only-if-condition), for example [if there is not already an item] (dynamodb-conditional-write-use-cases) with that key.

**Catch a concurrent change.** With optimistic locking, each item has a [version attribute that increments with every update] (dynamodb-optimistic-locking-detects-conflicts-at-write); a writer with an old version gets a [`ConditionalCheckFailedException`] (dynamodb-optimistic-locking-condition-fails-on-concurrent-change).

**Change several items as one.** A transaction makes [all-or-nothing changes to multiple items] (dynamodb-transactions-acid-multiple-items-tables) with [atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability (ACID)] (dynamodb-transactions-acid-multiple-items-tables); `TransactWriteItems` groups [up to 100 write actions] (dynamodb-transactwrite-100-actions).

**Stay in one account and Region.** The items must be in the [same AWS account and in the same Region] (dynamodb-transactwriteitems-same-account-same-region), and DynamoDB performs [two underlying reads or writes of every item] (dynamodb-transactions-no-extra-cost-two-operations).
plan.table: Which write keeps data correct (columns: Need | Use | If the check fails): create an item only if it is new | `PutItem` with a condition | the write fails; nothing changes; update only the version you read | a condition on the version attribute | the write fails, and you read again; change two items together | `TransactWriteItems` | [no changes are made at all] (dynamodb-transactwriteitems-vs-batchwriteitem); count page views | an atomic counter in `UpdateItem` | not a check: [the updates are not idempotent] (dynamodb-atomic-counter-not-idempotent).
plan.why: Why no locks? Optimistic locking [detects conflicts at write time] (dynamodb-optimistic-locking-detects-conflicts-at-write) instead of blocking readers, so no reader waits for a writer.
plan.exam_signal: "all-or-nothing" or "both updates must succeed or neither" points to `TransactWriteItems`, which gives a [guaranteed all-or-nothing result] (dynamodb-transactwriteitems-all-or-nothing).
plan.exam_trap_text: > **Exam trap:** `BatchWriteItem` is not a transaction. With it, [only some of the actions] (dynamodb-transactwriteitems-vs-batchwriteitem) might succeed, and [`BatchWriteItem` does not support `UpdateItem` requests] (dynamodb-batchwriteitem-no-updateitem). <!-- trap: dynamodb-trap-batch-write-is-atomic -->
plan.try_it: dynamodb-t03 (Try it callout, one line: 'Make a conditional write refuse an overwrite' in 3-do.md)
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence: a retried `TransactWriteItems` stays idempotent if you [include a client token] (dynamodb-transactwriteitems-idempotent-client-token), which is valid for [10 minutes] (dynamodb-transaction-client-token-10-minutes). Reference only: an atomic counter is wrong where [overcounting or undercounting can't be tolerated] (dynamodb-atomic-counter-not-for-exact-counts); transaction limits [100 unique items] (dynamodb-transaction-max-items) and [4 MB] (dynamodb-transaction-max-data) are in the B-list; [Transactions cannot be performed using indexes] (dynamodb-transactions-not-on-indexes); a failed transaction still uses capacity (dynamodb-transactions-capacity-consumed-even-on-failure).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: a condition or a transaction protects a write. The thing to watch is that a batch write can half succeed.
plan.stop_and_answer: A booking service must create a booking item and lower the seats-left number in another item. If one change fails, neither may stay. Which call? Answer: `TransactWriteItems`: the actions [either succeeds or fails as a unit] (dynamodb-transactwriteitems-succeeds-or-fails-as-unit) (write the link so the sentence reads 'the transaction either succeeds or fails as a unit'); add a condition that seats left stay above zero.

sections.heading: Time to Live deletes expired items without using write capacity

plan.problem: Old session and job items fill a table and raise the storage bill. A nightly delete job costs write capacity, and someone must run it.
trace: **Turn it on and name an attribute.** You [first enable it on a table] (dynamodb-ttl-enable-then-define-attribute) and then [define a specific attribute] (dynamodb-ttl-enable-then-define-attribute) for the expiry time.

**Store a number in epoch seconds.** The value must be a Number in [Unix epoch time format at the seconds granularity] (dynamodb-ttl-attribute-number-epoch-seconds); a TTL attribute that is [not a Number type] (dynamodb-ttl-non-number-attribute-ignored) is [ignored by the TTL process] (dynamodb-ttl-non-number-attribute-ignored).

**Delete later, at no write cost.** DynamoDB deletes expired items [within a few days of their expiration time] (dynamodb-ttl-deletes-within-days-no-wcu), [without consuming any write throughput] (dynamodb-faq-ttl-no-write-throughput).

**Filter until then.** Expired items [continue to show in read and write operations] (dynamodb-ttl-expired-items-visible-until-deleted) and [still count towards storage and read costs] (dynamodb-ttl-expired-items-count-for-storage-reads); they [can be filtered from read and write operations] (dynamodb-ttl-filter-expired-items-on-read).

**Send deletes to the stream.** TTL deletes [go into DynamoDB Streams] (dynamodb-ttl-deletes-appear-in-streams-as-service) as [service deletions instead of user deletes] (dynamodb-ttl-deletes-appear-in-streams-as-service), so a function can archive them.
plan.table: Keep or delete old data (columns: Need | Use): delete items after a time | time to live (TTL); keep rarely read data at a lower storage price | the Standard-IA table class, made for tables where [storage is the dominant cost] (dynamodb-table-class-standard-ia-lower-storage-cost); keep data until you delete it | nothing: by default data will [remain in the table indefinitely] (dynamodb-faq-data-retention-indefinite); archive expired items to Amazon S3 | TTL plus a stream and a Lambda function.
plan.why: Why days and not seconds? TTL runs as a background process: AWS presents it as a [cost-effective method for deleting items] (dynamodb-ttl-cost-effective-delete), not as a timer.
plan.exam_signal: "delete session data automatically after a period, at no extra cost" points to TTL, which [automatically deletes expired items] (dynamodb-faq-ttl-deletes-expired-items).
plan.spot_the_bug: **Spot the bug.** A team enables TTL on the attribute `expires`. The code writes it as text, for example "2026-10-14T12:00:00Z". A month later, no item has been deleted. What is wrong? Reveal: the TTL attribute must be a Number in [Unix epoch time format at the seconds granularity] (dynamodb-ttl-attribute-number-epoch-seconds); an attribute that is [not a Number type] (dynamodb-ttl-non-number-attribute-ignored) is [ignored by the TTL process] (dynamodb-ttl-non-number-attribute-ignored). Store the expiry as epoch seconds.
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence: Standard-IA has [~60% lower] (dynamodb-table-class-ia-60-lower-25-higher) storage cost and [~25% higher] (dynamodb-table-class-ia-60-lower-25-higher) read and write cost, and a table can switch [twice in a 30-day period] (dynamodb-faq-table-class-switch-twice-30-days). The 60/25 fact is volatile: prose only. Reference only: the time series pattern (dynamodb-time-series-old-tables-standard-ia); TTL toggle once per hour (dynamodb-ttl-toggle-once-per-hour); TTL more than five years in the past (dynamodb-ttl-five-years-past-ignored).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: TTL deletes old items for free in the background. The thing to watch is that expired items can still appear for a while.
plan.stop_and_answer: A game keeps daily scores for one year. After a week the scores are rarely read, and storage is most of the table bill. TTL, a table class, or both? Answer: both: the Standard-IA class, because [Standard-IA tables have lower storage costs] (dynamodb-faq-table-class-cost-tradeoff), and TTL to delete each score when its year ends, [without consuming any write throughput] (dynamodb-faq-ttl-no-write-throughput).

sections.heading: DynamoDB Streams records each item change in order for 24 hours

plan.problem: Other systems must react when an item changes. Reading the table again and again to find changes is slow and costs reads.
trace: **Turn on a stream.** DynamoDB Streams is an [optional feature that captures data modification events] (dynamodb-streams-optional-feature); it [operates asynchronously] (dynamodb-streams-no-performance-impact-on-enable), with [no performance impact on a table] (dynamodb-streams-no-performance-impact-on-enable).

**Choose what each record holds.** The stream view type is [`KEYS_ONLY`] (dynamodb-streams-view-keys-only), [`NEW_IMAGE`] (dynamodb-streams-view-new-image), [`OLD_IMAGE`] (dynamodb-streams-view-old-image) or [`NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES`] (dynamodb-streams-view-new-and-old-images); to change it, you [disable the current stream] (dynamodb-streams-view-type-not-editable) and create a new one.

**Keep each item's order.** Each record appears [exactly once in the stream] (dynamodb-streams-record-exactly-once), with [ordering at the level of an individual item] (dynamodb-streams-order-per-item-not-partition), [not across an entire partition] (dynamodb-streams-order-per-item-not-partition).

**Let Lambda read it.** DynamoDB is [integrated with AWS Lambda] (dynamodb-streams-lambda-triggers): triggers [automatically respond to events in DynamoDB Streams] (dynamodb-streams-lambda-triggers) through an [Event source mapping] (lambda-trigger-dynamodb-esm), and on an error [Lambda retries the batch] (dynamodb-streams-lambda-retries-until-success-or-expiry).
**Lose records after a day.** Stream records have a [lifetime of 24 hours] (dynamodb-stream-records-24-hours) and are then [automatically removed from the stream] (dynamodb-stream-records-24-hours).
plan.table: DynamoDB Streams or Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB (columns: Question | DynamoDB Streams | Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB): consumers per shard | [2 simultaneous] (dynamodb-streams-vs-kds-consumers-per-shard) | [5 simultaneous] (dynamodb-streams-vs-kds-consumers-per-shard), or [20 simultaneous consumers per shard] (dynamodb-streams-vs-kds-consumers-per-shard) with enhanced fan-out; duplicates | [No duplicate records appear in the stream] (dynamodb-streams-vs-kds-duplicates) | [Duplicate records might occasionally appear in the stream] (dynamodb-streams-vs-kds-duplicates); order | [same sequence as the actual modifications] (dynamodb-streams-vs-kds-ordering) | from a [timestamp attribute on each stream record] (dynamodb-streams-vs-kds-ordering). Retention stays out of this table: the Exam trap carries it.

sections.heading: DAX answers repeated eventually consistent reads from memory in microseconds

plan.problem: Single-digit milliseconds is not fast enough for some screens, and a few hot items can get most of the reads. A cache in front of the table answers those reads from memory.
trace: **Send every call to DAX.** The DAX client [directs all of your application's DynamoDB API requests] (dax-client-routes-requests-to-cluster) to the cluster, and DAX is [API-compatible with DynamoDB] (dax-api-compatible-minimal-changes).

**Answer a hit from memory.** DAX keeps an [item cache] (dax-item-cache-getitem-batchgetitem) for GetItem and a [query cache] (dax-query-cache-query-scan) for Query and Scan, and returns [eventually consistent data] (dax-eventually-consistent-microsecond-latency) [with microsecond latency] (dax-eventually-consistent-microsecond-latency).

**Fill the cache on a miss.** On a miss, [DAX sends the request to DynamoDB] (dax-cache-miss-reads-dynamodb-and-fills-cache), and then [DAX stores them in the item cache] (dax-cache-miss-reads-dynamodb-and-fills-cache).
**Write through.** DAX is a [write-through caching service] (dax-is-write-through-cache): data is [first written to the DynamoDB table] (dax-write-through-both-table-and-dax), then to the cache.

**Skip the cache for strong reads.** [DAX passes strongly consistent read requests to DynamoDB] (dax-passes-through-strong-reads-and-transactions), and [it does not cache the results] (dax-passes-through-strong-reads-and-transactions).
plan.table: When DAX helps (columns: Workload | DAX?): many repeated reads of the same items | yes: it suits apps that [read a small number of items more frequently] (dax-ideal-fastest-reads-hot-keys); reads that must be strongly consistent | no gain: apps that [require strongly consistent reads] (dax-not-ideal-strong-reads-write-heavy-few-repeats) are not ideal; write-heavy | little: [DAX benefits might be limited] (dax-write-heavy-limited-benefit); modest latency needs | not needed: DynamoDB alone gives [single-digit millisecond performance] (dax-modest-needs-use-dynamodb-alone).
plan.why: Why a cluster in your VPC? DAX is designed to [run within an Amazon Virtual Private Cloud] (dax-runs-inside-vpc), and [Three nodes are required] (dax-production-three-nodes-three-azs) for a fault-tolerant cluster.
plan.exam_signal: "microsecond reads from DynamoDB with minimal code changes" points to DAX, which needs [only minimal functional changes] (dax-api-compatible-minimal-changes); "cache several databases, or use lists and sorted sets" points to ElastiCache: [ElastiCache (Redis OSS) supports advanced data structures] (dax-vs-elasticache-complex-queries).
plan.diagram: dynamodb-dax-read (after the trace; caption and steps in diagrams)
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence: cached items stay until their TTL, by default [5 minutes] (dax-default-ttl-5-minutes-both-caches), so a write that bypasses DAX leaves the cache and the table to [hold inconsistent values for the same key] (dax-bypass-causes-inconsistent-values) until then. Never link dax-can-subvert-dynamodb-iam-policies: its display holds bold markup. Reference only: cluster size limits (dax-cluster-up-to-11-nodes, B-list), port 8111 (dax-security-group-port-8111), same-Region tables (dax-same-region-as-tables), encryption at rest without customer keys (dax-encryption-at-rest-no-customer-keys).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: DAX answers repeated reads from memory. The thing to watch is strong reads, which go straight to the table.
plan.stop_and_answer: A leaderboard reads the same 100 items thousands of times a second with eventually consistent reads; writes are rare. Latency must drop to microseconds with almost no code change. Does DAX fit? Answer: yes; DAX is [API-compatible with DynamoDB] (dax-api-compatible-minimal-changes), and it delivers [up to a 10 times performance improvement] (dax-faq-microsecond-cache-10x) for repeated reads. 100 is an example value in the prompt.

sections.heading: Every restore, from a backup or a point in time, creates a new table

plan.problem: A bad release deletes items, or someone deletes a table. The data must come back as it was at a known moment, without risk to what still works.
trace: **Take on-demand backups.** Each on-demand backup means the [entire table data is backed up] (dynamodb-backup-full-table-every-time), [without consuming any provisioned throughput on the table] (dynamodb-backup-no-provisioned-throughput) and with [zero impact on table performance or availability] (dynamodb-backup-restore-zero-performance-impact).

**Turn on point-in-time recovery.** PITR gives [automatic continuous backups] (dynamodb-pitr-automatic-continuous-backups) that protect a table [from accidental write or delete operations] (dynamodb-pitr-protects-accidental-writes-deletes); you can restore to a moment from [five minutes before the current time] (dynamodb-pitr-restore-window-five-minutes-to-period) back to the start of the recovery period.

**Restore into a new table.** Point-in-time recovery [always restores to a new table] (dynamodb-pitr-restores-to-new-table), and a backup restores the [entire table data to a new table] (dynamodb-backup-restore-only-to-new-table).

**Set the missing settings again.** [Tags aren't preserved in restored tables] (dynamodb-restore-tags-not-preserved); add them, and check the other table settings, before the application uses the table.

**Copy to other accounts and Regions.** AWS Backup can [copy backups to multiple AWS accounts] (dynamodb-aws-backup-copy-multiple-accounts-regions) [as part of a scheduled backup plan] (dynamodb-aws-backup-copy-multiple-accounts-regions), and Vault Lock keeps them [write-once-read-many (WORM)] (dynamodb-aws-backup-vault-lock-worm).
plan.table: Recovery options (columns: Option | RPO | RTO): PITR | [minimal RPO (seconds)] (dynamodb-dr-pitr-rpo-seconds) | [reasonable RTO (minutes to hours)] (dynamodb-dr-pitr-rpo-seconds); daily on-demand backup | [RPO of 24 hours] (dynamodb-dr-daily-on-demand-backup-rpo-24h) | minutes to hours; AWS Backup with an hourly cross-Region copy | [RPO of 1 hour] (dynamodb-dr-aws-backup-rpo-1-hour) | minutes to hours; export to Amazon S3 | [RPO of a few minutes] (dynamodb-dr-s3-export-rpo-minutes) | minutes to hours. 'minutes to hours' without a link in the last three rows is plain text with no number: allowed. Spell out RPO and RTO at first use (bank terms).
plan.why: Why always a new table? A restore never touches the live table: you check the restored data first, then point the application at it or copy items back. The resiliency of your data stays your job ([managing resiliency of your data including backup, versioning, and replication strategies] (well-architected-resiliency-managed-services-customer-owns-backup-versioning-replication)).
plan.exam_signal: "restore the table to the state just before an accidental delete" points to point-in-time recovery, whose latest restore point is typically [five minutes before the current time] (dynamodb-pitr-latest-restorable-five-minutes).
plan.exam_trap_text: > **Exam trap:** A restore does not roll the live table back. You [can't overwrite an existing table] (dynamodb-restore-cannot-overwrite-existing-table) during a restore, so the application must switch to the new table or copy the items back. <!-- trap: dynamodb-trap-restore-in-place -->
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: deleted tables, exports and the recovery period (at most 70 words). Deleting a table that has PITR leaves a [system backup] (dynamodb-pitr-deleted-table-system-backup) that DynamoDB [retains it for 35 days] (dynamodb-pitr-deleted-table-system-backup). Turning PITR off and on will [reset the start time] (dynamodb-pitr-reenable-resets-start-time). Export to Amazon S3 needs PITR ([enable PITR on your table] (dynamodb-export-requires-pitr)) and exports [both full and incremental data] (dynamodb-export-full-and-incremental). The recovery period can be set [between 1 and 35 days] (dynamodb-change-pitr-configurable-period-2025-01).
plan.body_extras: Reference only, no sentence: cross-Region PITR restore (dynamodb-pitr-cross-region-restore); AWS Backup restores to another Region need a copy first (dynamodb-aws-backup-restore-needs-copy-first); import from S3 creates a new table and uses no write capacity (dynamodb-import-new-table-only, dynamodb-import-no-write-capacity); PITR on each global table replica (dynamodb-faq-global-tables-pitr-per-replica).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: every restore builds a new table. The thing to watch is that your application must switch to it.
plan.stop_and_answer: A bank requires backups that an administrator cannot delete, with copies in a second account. What do you use? Answer: AWS Backup: it can [copy backups to multiple AWS accounts] (dynamodb-aws-backup-copy-multiple-accounts-regions), and Vault Lock [protects backups from inadvertent or malicious delete operations] (dynamodb-aws-backup-vault-lock-worm).

sections.heading: In a global table, every replica accepts reads and writes

plan.problem: Users on two continents want low latency, and the service must survive the loss of a whole Region. A table in one Region cannot give either.
trace: **Add a replica table per Region.** A global table has [two or more replica tables] (dynamodb-global-table-one-replica-per-region) in different Regions, with [only one replica per AWS Region] (dynamodb-global-table-one-replica-per-region).

**Write anywhere.** [Any global table replica] (dynamodb-global-table-any-replica-serves-reads-writes) can [serve reads and writes] (dynamodb-global-table-any-replica-serves-reads-writes), and DynamoDB [automatically replicates the write to all other replicas] (dynamodb-global-table-write-replicated-automatically).

**Replicate eventually by default.** If you choose nothing, the table [defaults to multi-Region eventual consistency (MREC)] (dynamodb-global-tables-default-mrec); writes arrive [typically within a second or less] (dynamodb-gt-mrec-default-last-writer-wins), and a conflict ends with [last writer wins] (dynamodb-gt-mrec-default-last-writer-wins).

**Fail over without the database.** A global table has [no primary Region] (dynamodb-faq-global-tables-no-failover-needed); when a Region is impaired, you [shift application traffic to a different Region] (dynamodb-global-tables-shift-traffic-on-regional-impairment).

**Know the recovery numbers.** MREC gives an [RPO of a few seconds] (dynamodb-dr-global-tables-mrec-rto-zero) and an [RTO of zero] (dynamodb-dr-global-tables-mrec-rto-zero); the SLA is [99.999%] (dynamodb-gt-sla-99999-vs-single-region-9999) instead of [99.99%] (dynamodb-gt-sla-99999-vs-single-region-9999) for one Region.
plan.table: MREC or MRSC (columns: Question | MREC | MRSC): Regions | two or more | [exactly three Regions] (dynamodb-gt-mrsc-exactly-three-regions); data loss after a Region failure | [RPO of a few seconds] (dynamodb-dr-global-tables-mrec-rto-zero) | [zero RPO] (dynamodb-dr-global-tables-mrsc-rpo-zero); a strongly consistent read after a write in another Region | can return [stale data returned from strongly consistent read operations] (dynamodb-mrec-strong-reads-may-be-stale) | returns the latest version. The MRSC facts dynamodb-gt-mrsc-* are volatile (MRSC is new since 2025-06-30): table and prose only, never a question key. Write MRSC's last cell 'the latest version' as plain text or link [always return the latest version of an item] (dynamodb-gt-mrsc-synchronous-latest-reads).
plan.why: Why last writer wins? Both models use [multi-Region writes, asynchronous replication, last-writer-wins conflict resolution] (dynamodb-global-tables-both-models-same-features) in MREC tables, so two Regions can change one item at once, and one simple rule keeps every replica table equal. If this link text is too long for the sentence, link [last writer wins] (dynamodb-gt-mrec-default-last-writer-wins) instead.
plan.exam_signal: "active-active in several Regions with local writes" points to global tables, a [multi-Region, and multi-active database] (dynamodb-faq-global-tables-multi-active); "one writer Region, relational" points to Aurora Global Database, where [Only the primary cluster performs write operations] (dynamodb-vs-aurora-global-database-single-writer).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: what does not cross Regions (at most 70 words). Transactions are [not supported across Regions] (dynamodb-transaction-not-across-gt-regions); in MREC, transactional writes are [not replicated as a unit across Regions] (dynamodb-mrec-transactions-not-replicated-as-unit). In MRSC, [Time to Live (TTL) is not supported] (dynamodb-gt-mrsc-no-ttl-lsi-transactions) (volatile: Go deeper only). You [cannot change a global table's consistency mode] (dynamodb-global-tables-consistency-mode-fixed) after you create it.
plan.body_extras: Reference only, no sentence unless words remain: no cross-Region data transfer fee for replication (dynamodb-gt-no-cross-region-transfer-fee); replicated writes are billed in each replica Region (dynamodb-gt-rwru-per-replica); provisioned replicas need write capacity for replication (dynamodb-gt-provisioned-replication-uses-write-capacity); multi-account global tables (MREC only; volatile change fact): no sentence; the product page's 'one to two seconds' disagrees with the guide's 'a second or less': write one figure only, the guide's, linked above.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: every Region can read and write the same table. The thing to watch is conflicts, where the last write wins.
plan.stop_and_answer: A global table has replica tables in us-east-1 and eu-west-1. us-east-1 is impaired. What must the team change in the database to keep writing? Answer: nothing in the database: there is [no primary Region] (dynamodb-faq-global-tables-no-failover-needed); route users to eu-west-1, and data not yet replicated [will be replicated when the replica becomes healthy] (dynamodb-mrec-unreplicated-data-resumes-after-recovery).

sections.heading: IAM controls access, and every table is encrypted at rest

plan.problem: A table often holds personal data. Only the right workloads may read it, the data must be encrypted, and traffic from private subnets should stay off the internet.
trace: **Use IAM, not passwords.** DynamoDB has [no user names or passwords] (dynamodb-no-passwords-iam-access); IAM policies decide every request.

**Narrow to items and attributes.** A policy can [restrict access to individual items in a table] (dynamodb-fgac-restrict-items-and-attributes) and [access to the attributes in those items] (dynamodb-fgac-restrict-items-and-attributes), for example with the condition key [`LeadingKeys`] (dynamodb-leadingkeys-condition-key-partition-key), which stands for [the partition key] (dynamodb-leadingkeys-condition-key-partition-key).

**Encrypt by default.** [By default, DynamoDB encrypts] (dynamodb-encrypt-at-rest-default) all data at rest; you choose an [AWS owned key (default encryption type)] (dynamodb-encryption-key-types), an [AWS managed key] (dynamodb-encryption-key-types) or a [Customer managed key] (dynamodb-encryption-key-types).

**Keep control of your key.** With a customer managed key, disabling the key [prevents all users and the DynamoDB service] (dynamodb-customer-managed-key-disabled-blocks-access) from reading or writing the table.

**Take the private path.** A gateway endpoint lets a VPC reach DynamoDB [without requiring an internet gateway or NAT device] (dynamodb-faq-gateway-endpoint-no-igw-nat); from on premises, [you must use AWS PrivateLink] (dynamodb-faq-gateway-endpoint-limits-use-privatelink).
plan.table: Which key type (columns: Key | Cost | What you can do): AWS owned key | [offered at no additional charge] (dynamodb-aws-owned-key-no-additional-charge) | nothing: you [cannot view, manage, or use AWS owned keys] (dynamodb-aws-owned-key-not-viewable); AWS managed key | [AWS KMS charges apply] (dynamodb-aws-owned-key-no-additional-charge) | [audit their use in AWS CloudTrail logs] (dynamodb-aws-managed-key-audit-cloudtrail); customer managed key | KMS charges (plain words, already linked in row 2) | [Customer managed keys] (dynamodb-faq-key-customer-managed-most-control) give the most control: you create, rotate and disable them.
plan.why: Why IAM and not database users? DynamoDB is an API service: [DynamoDB utilizes IAM] (dynamodb-no-passwords-iam-access), so the role that runs your code also carries its table permissions.
plan.exam_signal: "each user may read only the items with the user's own ID" points to fine-grained access control with the [`LeadingKeys`] (dynamodb-leadingkeys-condition-key-partition-key) condition key.
plan.spot_the_bug: **Spot the bug.** Lambda functions in private subnets write to DynamoDB through a NAT gateway, and the NAT bill grows each month. What is wrong? Reveal: the functions can reach DynamoDB through a gateway endpoint, [without requiring an internet gateway or NAT device] (dynamodb-faq-gateway-endpoint-no-igw-nat); there is [no additional charge for using gateway endpoints] (vpc-endpoints-wp-gateway-endpoint-no-additional-charge).
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence: DynamoDB [supports resource-based policies for tables and streams] (dynamodb-faq-resource-policies-tables-streams), and Block Public Access is [always enabled with DynamoDB] (dynamodb-faq-block-public-access-always-on). Reference only: traffic uses HTTPS (dynamodb-https-default-ssl-tls); encryption covers indexes, streams and backups (dynamodb-encryption-covers-indexes-streams-backups); the volatile resource-policy and ABAC change facts: no sentence; chapter 10 and chapter 11 own the endpoint details (xref).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: IAM controls access, and encryption is on by default. The thing to watch is the network path from private subnets.
plan.stop_and_answer: The security team disables the customer managed key of a table during an incident and forgets it. What happens to the application, and what happens after a week? Answer: reads and writes fail at once, because the disabled key [prevents all users and the DynamoDB service] (dynamodb-customer-managed-key-disabled-blocks-access); if the key stays inaccessible [longer than seven days] (dynamodb-customer-managed-key-inaccessible-archived), [the table is archived] (dynamodb-customer-managed-key-inaccessible-archived).

sections.heading: FAQ quick-fire
sections.plan: Ten items **FAQ 1.** to **FAQ 10.** in the form of CONVENTIONS D12 (see faq): a can-or-cannot question, a reveal with the short answer and its fact link, and an AWS quote block with the quote given, copied exactly, and the link line '— [Amazon DynamoDB FAQs](https://aws.amazon.com/dynamodb/faqs/)'. At most 430 words.

traps.belief: If the table as a whole has unused capacity, no request is throttled.
traps.truth: Each partition has its own ceiling of 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units per second, so traffic on one hot key or item is throttled while the rest of the table is idle.

traps.belief: A read right after a write always returns the new value.
traps.truth: Eventually consistent is the default for every read, and it might not reflect a write that just finished; set ConsistentRead to true on the table or an LSI to get the latest data.

traps.belief: Time to Live deletes an item at the second it expires, so expired items never appear in reads.
traps.truth: DynamoDB deletes expired items within a few days of their expiration time; until then they still show in reads, so filter them out.

traps.belief: DAX speeds up every read, strongly consistent reads included.
traps.truth: DAX passes strongly consistent reads to DynamoDB and does not cache the results; it serves eventually consistent data.

traps.belief: A global table has a primary Region, and a Region outage needs a database failover to a secondary.
traps.truth: A global table has no primary Region; any replica table serves reads and writes, so no database failover is required.

traps.belief: A global secondary index can serve strongly consistent reads, like the table.
traps.truth: Strongly consistent reads are supported only on tables and local secondary indexes; queries on a global secondary index are eventually consistent only.

traps.belief: An on-demand table absorbs any traffic spike instantly, however large.
traps.truth: On-demand instantly accommodates up to double the previous peak; traffic above double the previous peak within 30 minutes can be throttled, so pre-warm the table for a larger launch.

traps.belief: Auto scaling on a provisioned table prevents throttling, even in a sudden spike.
traps.truth: Auto scaling reacts after the target is breached for two consecutive minutes and takes several minutes to update capacity; throttling can occur regardless of auto scaling.

traps.belief: A filter expression on a Scan or Query lowers the read capacity that the request consumes.
traps.truth: A filter is applied after the items are read, so the request consumes the same read capacity with or without it.

traps.belief: You can add a local secondary index to a table that already holds data.
traps.truth: Local secondary indexes are created only when the table is created; to add an index later, create a global secondary index.

traps.belief: BatchWriteItem writes all of its items or none of them.
traps.truth: With BatchWriteItem only some of the actions might succeed; TransactWriteItems is all-or-nothing.

traps.belief: A DynamoDB stream keeps item changes for as long as consumers need them, like an archive.
traps.truth: Stream records have a lifetime of 24 hours; Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB keeps records up to 1 year for replay.

traps.belief: A point-in-time restore or a backup restore rolls the existing table back in place.
traps.truth: Every restore creates a new table, and a restore cannot overwrite an existing table; the application switches to the new table or items are copied back.

traps.belief: A DAX cluster in front of a table absorbs the write traffic, so writes are no longer throttled and the table costs less.
traps.truth: DAX is a write-through cache: data is first written to the DynamoDB table, and for a write-heavy application DAX benefits might be limited.

traps.belief: On-demand capacity mode is always the cheaper mode, because you pay only for the requests you make.
traps.truth: On-demand costs less when the average utilization of provisioned capacity is below 35%; a steady and predictable workload is the ideal workload for provisioned capacity.

traps.belief: Returning fewer attributes with a projection expression lowers the read capacity that a Scan consumes.
traps.truth: A Scan consumes read capacity by the number and size of the items it reads, not by the amount of data it returns.

traps.belief: Each read or write uses one capacity unit, whatever the size of the item.
traps.truth: A write capacity unit covers one write per second for an item up to 1 KB, and item sizes round up to the next 1 KB multiple for writes and the next 4 KB multiple for reads, so a larger item uses more units.

traps.belief: A backup copied to another Region lets users keep reading and writing there at once when the first Region fails.
traps.truth: A backup is restored into a new table first, and hourly AWS Backup copies give an RPO of 1 hour; reads and writes in another Region at once need a global table, with an RTO of zero.

faq.q: Can one global table have two replica tables in the same Region?
faq.answer: No; a global table has [one replica table per AWS Region] (dynamodb-faq-global-table-one-replica-per-region)
faq.quote: A single Amazon DynamoDB global table can only have one replica table per AWS Region.

faq.q: Does a global table need a database failover when a Region fails?
faq.answer: No; it has [no primary Region] (dynamodb-faq-global-tables-no-failover-needed), so you send traffic to another Region
faq.quote: A global table has no primary Region, and thus no database failover is required when directing read and write traffic to a different Region.

faq.q: Can you store large images inside DynamoDB items?
faq.answer: You can store binary data, but the better pattern is to [store pointers to Amazon S3 objects] (dynamodb-faq-blob-use-s3-pointers)
faq.quote: Yes, DynamoDB can store BLOB; however, it is not generally suited to storing documents or images. A better architectural pattern is to store pointers to Amazon S3 objects in a DynamoDB table.

faq.q: Does a time to live (TTL) delete use write capacity?
faq.answer: No; DynamoDB deletes the item [without consuming any write throughput] (dynamodb-faq-ttl-no-write-throughput)
faq.quote: With TTL, you can define a per-item timestamp to determine when an item is no longer needed, and DynamoDB automatically deletes the item from your table without consuming any write throughput.

faq.q: Does DynamoDB delete old data by itself?
faq.answer: No; data will [remain in the table indefinitely] (dynamodb-faq-data-retention-indefinite) unless you or TTL delete it
faq.quote: There is no set expiration or deletion time for data stored in an Amazon DynamoDB table by default.

faq.q: Can you query on attributes that are not part of the primary key?
faq.answer: Yes, through [global secondary indexes and local secondary indexes] (dynamodb-faq-query-nonkey-via-gsi-lsi)
faq.quote: DynamoDB also provides flexible querying by letting you query on nonprimary key attributes using global secondary indexes and local secondary indexes.

faq.q: Does Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB keep record order and remove duplicates?
faq.answer: No; it [does not provide record ordering nor deduplication guarantees] (dynamodb-faq-kinesis-no-ordering-dedup); DynamoDB Streams does
faq.quote: Unlike DynamoDB Streams, Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB does not provide record ordering nor deduplication guarantees.

faq.q: Can a VPC reach DynamoDB without an internet gateway or a NAT device?
faq.answer: Yes, through a gateway endpoint, [without requiring an internet gateway or NAT device] (dynamodb-faq-gateway-endpoint-no-igw-nat)
faq.quote: With a gateway endpoint, you can access DynamoDB from your VPC, without requiring an internet gateway or NAT device for your VPC.

faq.q: Can on-premises servers use a DynamoDB gateway endpoint?
faq.answer: No; for on-premises access [you must use AWS PrivateLink] (dynamodb-faq-gateway-endpoint-limits-use-privatelink)
faq.quote: However, gateway endpoints do not allow access from on-premises networks, from peered VPCs in other AWS Regions, or through a transit gateway.

faq.q: Can you switch a table between the Standard and Standard-IA table classes?
faq.answer: Yes, [twice in a 30-day period] (dynamodb-faq-table-class-switch-twice-30-days), without downtime
faq.quote: You can switch between these table classes twice in a 30-day period without downtime, allowing you to optimize your costs based on your table's usage patterns.

reasons_with_facts: Option 1 keeps the bottleneck: functions open connections to a relational server, while [DynamoDB uses an HTTP API] (lambda-ddb-http-api-no-connections) and needs none; a larger instance still holds every row lock in one place.

Option 3 risks the data: ElastiCache is an [ephemeral cache for frequently accessed data] (dynamodb-decision-guide-elasticache-caching-layer), and relying on cached data [as if it is durably stored] (dynamodb-wa-cache-not-durable-store) is an anti-pattern; job state must survive.

Option 2: on-demand mode can [handle fluctuating traffic] (dynamodb-ondemand-better-for-fluctuating-traffic) with no capacity to set; reads and writes by call ID are key lookups; the GSI gives the second access pattern because its [index key schema can be different] (dynamodb-gsi-key-schema-can-differ); TTL deletes old jobs [without consuming any write throughput] (dynamodb-faq-ttl-no-write-throughput).

question_slots.note: Shared stem: a company stores order data in a DynamoDB table in provisioned capacity mode with auto scaling. The company wants to keep reads and writes from being throttled and to lower the table's cost. Changed phrase: 'Traffic is unpredictable: it stays near zero for hours, then rises to many times the usual level within minutes.' Ask: 'Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?' Key: (A) Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode ([On-demand capacity mode is the better choice] (dynamodb-ondemand-better-for-fluctuating-traffic); [billed per read or write request] (dynamodb-ondemand-billed-per-request-zero-traffic-free)). Options identical in q07: (A) as above; (B) Keep provisioned capacity with auto scaling, and buy reserved capacity for the base load; (C) Put a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster in front of the table; (D) Set the provisioned capacity to the highest peak ever measured and keep it there. In q01, (B) carries the trap dynamodb-trap-auto-scaling-prevents-throttling (why links [does not respond instantly] (dynamodb-throttling-with-autoscaling-possible)); (C) is misconception: DAX caches reads and [DAX benefits might be limited] (dax-write-heavy-limited-benefit) for writes; (D) violates-qualifier (pays for the peak all day: [hourly read and write capacity you have provisioned] (dynamodb-provisioned-billing-basis)). Write option texts in neutral words that fit both stems. Do not use the volatile 2024-11-01 price change in any why.

A company stores votes in a DynamoDB table in provisioned mode. The partition key is the contest ID, and during a final almost every vote is for one contest. CloudWatch shows that consumed write capacity is far below the table's provisioned write capacity, but many writes are throttled. Which solution will BEST resolve the throttling? Key: spread the writes for the hot contest over several partition key values by adding a random suffix (write sharding), and sum the shards when reading ([add a random number] (dynamodb-write-sharding-random-suffix); spread the writes [across more distinct partition key values] (dynamodb-few-partition-keys-spread-writes)). Distractors: raise the table's provisioned write capacity (trap dynamodb-trap-spare-capacity-no-throttle; why links [1,000 write units per second] (dynamodb-partition-max-throughput)); switch the table to on-demand capacity mode (misconception: on-demand does not raise the per-partition ceiling; why links [throttling while other operations may remain underutilized] (dynamodb-hot-partitions-throttle-while-others-underutilized) and states that the partition ceiling applies to every partition; the claims reviewer checks this wording); add a DAX cluster (violates-requirement: DAX helps reads, [DAX benefits might be limited] (dax-write-heavy-limited-benefit) for writes). Worked think-aloud: find the constraint (one hot key, spare table capacity), predict, eliminate, choose.

Difficulty 1, qualifier none (no violates-qualifier option). An application writes an order item to a DynamoDB table and reads it back at once with GetItem. Sometimes the read returns the old version. The read must always return the result of every earlier successful write. What should a solutions architect do? Key: set ConsistentRead to true on the GetItem call ([optional `ConsistentRead` parameter] (dynamodb-consistentread-parameter); [most up-to-date data] (dynamodb-consistentread-parameter)). Distractors: read the order from a global secondary index with a strongly consistent query (trap dynamodb-trap-gsi-strong-read; why links [support eventual consistency only] (dynamodb-index-read-consistency-gsi-vs-lsi)); add DAX so that reads come from memory (trap dynamodb-trap-dax-speeds-every-read; why links [DAX passes strongly consistent read requests to DynamoDB] (dax-passes-through-strong-reads-and-transactions) and [eventually consistent data] (dax-eventually-consistent-microsecond-latency)); enable DynamoDB Streams on the table (misconception: a stream feeds other consumers; reads from streams are eventually consistent: [reads from GSIs and streams are eventually consistent] (dynamodb-gsi-and-streams-reads-eventual)).

question_slots.note: Shared stem: a company's DynamoDB table orders has the partition key CustomerId and the sort key OrderDate. A new screen must list one customer's orders sorted by OrderTotal. Changed phrase: 'The table currently holds two years of orders, and eventually consistent reads are acceptable for the new screen.' Ask: 'Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?' Key: add a DAX cluster and use the DAX client for all reads: product pages use eventually consistent reads, which DAX serves from memory, and the checkout uses strongly consistent reads, which DAX passes to the table ([eventually consistent data] [with microsecond latency] (dax-eventually-consistent-microsecond-latency); [DAX passes strongly consistent read requests to DynamoDB] (dax-passes-through-strong-reads-and-transactions)). Distractors: make every read strongly consistent through DAX so that the checkout is fast too (trap dynamodb-trap-dax-speeds-every-read; why links [it does not cache the results] (dax-passes-through-strong-reads-and-transactions)); have the checkout read a global secondary index with strong consistency (trap dynamodb-trap-gsi-strong-read; why links [only supported on tables and local secondary indexes] (dynamodb-strong-reads-only-tables-and-lsi)); cache the product items in each web server's memory and refresh them every few seconds (violates-qualifier: code and stale copies per server; misconception tag none). Keys: enable TTL on an attribute that stores the expiry time as a Number in epoch seconds ([Unix epoch time format at the seconds granularity] (dynamodb-ttl-attribute-number-epoch-seconds); [without consuming any write throughput] (dynamodb-faq-ttl-no-write-throughput)); in every read, reject items whose expiry time is in the past, with a filter or a check in code ([can be filtered from read and write operations] (dynamodb-ttl-filter-expired-items-on-read)). Distractors: rely on TTL alone, because TTL deletes items as soon as they expire (trap dynamodb-trap-ttl-deletes-on-time; why links [within a few days of their expiration time] (dynamodb-ttl-deletes-within-days-no-wcu)); store the expiry as an ISO 8601 text string (misconception: [ignored by the TTL process] (dynamodb-ttl-non-number-attribute-ignored)); a Lambda function every minute that scans and deletes expired sessions (violates-requirement: write cost, overhead). Worked: no. 'one hour' is a stem value.
