speak.prompt: On-demand or provisioned capacity? I do not know my traffic yet.
speak.note: Ben talks in short technical sentences and wants the fewest moving parts. Short answer: start in on-demand mode; move to provisioned capacity once the traffic is steady and you can forecast it. How it works: on-demand bills each request and sets capacity for you; provisioned bills the reads and writes per second you set, used or not, and reserved capacity lowers that rate. Watch: on-demand follows up to double the previous peak at once; before a launch far above that, pre-warm the table. In your case: 'What does your busiest hour look like after the launch?' Must not say: 'on-demand has no limits'; 'provisioned is always cheaper'; 'you can never switch back'. Numbers as words from the say forms: double the previous peak; switching back to provisioned at any time. The four-per-day switch limit is volatile: say 'a few times a day', or leave it out.

speak.persona: a startup founder in office hours
speak.prompt: DynamoDB or PostgreSQL: which database should our new app start with?
speak.note: First sentence starts 'Both': both are managed, durable databases; the difference is how you ask for data. Short answer: DynamoDB if you know your access patterns and they are key lookups at scale; PostgreSQL if you need joins and new ad hoc queries. How it works: DynamoDB stores items by key and answers known patterns fast at any scale, with no servers and pay per request; PostgreSQL runs SQL with joins on instances you size. Watch: in DynamoDB you design the table from the questions it must answer, and a new question can need a new index. In your case: 'Can you list the five queries your app runs most?' Must not say: 'DynamoDB supports joins'; 'NoSQL means no schema at all'; 'PostgreSQL cannot scale'. Numbers as words: single-digit milliseconds.

speak.prompt: Our DynamoDB table shows spare capacity, but some writes are throttled. Why?
speak.note: Short answer: the capacity is spread over partitions, and one hot key is hitting one partition's ceiling. How it works: DynamoDB hashes the partition key to place each item; each partition serves up to three thousand reads and one thousand writes per second; when most writes go to one key, that partition throttles while others sit idle. Watch: raising table capacity does not fix it; spread the key, for example with a random suffix, or pick a key with many values. In your case: 'Which key gets the most writes, and can we split it?' Must not say: 'add more capacity'; 'switch to on-demand and it goes away'; 'DynamoDB has no limits'. Numbers as words: three thousand read units and one thousand write units per second.

speak.prompt: If the AWS Region we use goes down, do we lose our job records?
speak.note: Ana uses no AWS terms: explain a Region as 'one AWS location with several separate data centers' and an Availability Zone as 'one of those data centers' the first time. Short answer: a single data center failing loses nothing; a whole Region going down stops the service until it returns, unless we keep a copy in a second Region. How it works: each write is copied to three Availability Zones before DynamoDB confirms it; continuous backups let us restore a table; a global table later keeps a live copy in a second Region that can take over in seconds. Watch: the second Region doubles part of the database bill, so it waits for the bank's recovery requirement. In your case: 'How many minutes of downtime can our customers accept?' Must not say: 'the data is copied to another Region automatically'; 'a Region can never fail'; 'backups make us available during the outage'. Numbers as words: three Availability Zones; a few seconds of data.

cards.front: In DynamoDB, what is the maximum size of one item?
cards.back: 400 KB, attribute names included.

cards.front: In DynamoDB, what can one partition serve at most?
cards.back: 3,000 read units per second and 1,000 write units per second.

cards.front: In DynamoDB, how is the size of a read rounded?
cards.back: Up to the next 4 KB multiple.

cards.front: In DynamoDB, how is the size of a write rounded?
cards.back: Up to the next 1 KB multiple.

cards.front: In DynamoDB, how much data can one Query call return?
cards.back: 1 MB per call; continue with LastEvaluatedKey.

cards.front: In DynamoDB Streams, how long does a stream record live?
cards.back: A lifetime of 24 hours.

cards.front: In DynamoDB, how many local secondary indexes can one table have?
cards.back: Up to 5 local secondary indexes, defined with the table.

cards.front: In DynamoDB, how large can an item collection grow in a table with an LSI?
cards.back: 10 GB.

cards.front: In DynamoDB, which read is the default: eventually consistent or strongly consistent?
cards.back: Eventually consistent.

cards.front: In DynamoDB, a new app's traffic is unknown and spiky. Which capacity mode?
cards.back: On-demand capacity mode.

cards.front: In DynamoDB, can a global secondary index serve a strongly consistent read?
cards.back: No. GSI queries support eventual consistency only.

cards.front: In DynamoDB, does a filter expression lower the read capacity of a Scan?
cards.back: No. The Scan consumes the same amount of read capacity.

cards.front: In DynamoDB, two items must change together or not at all. Which API?
cards.back: TransactWriteItems.

cards.front: In a DynamoDB global table, does a Region outage need a database failover?
cards.back: No. A global table has no primary Region.

cards.front: In DynamoDB, can you add a local secondary index to an existing table?
cards.back: No. Add a global secondary index instead.

cards.front: DynamoDB Streams or Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB: which keeps records up to 1 year?
cards.back: Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB.

cards.front: In DynamoDB, does TTL delete an item at the moment it expires?
cards.back: No. Within a few days of their expiration time.

cards.front: In DAX, are strongly consistent reads cached?
cards.back: No. DAX passes them to DynamoDB.

cards.front: In DynamoDB, can a restore overwrite the existing table?
cards.back: No. Every restore creates a new table.

cards.front: In DynamoDB on-demand mode, is any spike absorbed at once?
cards.back: No. Up to double the previous peak; pre-warm for more.

cards.front: In DynamoDB, does auto scaling prevent throttling in a sudden spike?
cards.back: No. It does not respond instantly.

cards.front: In DynamoDB, one key gets most writes and is throttled. What do you change?
cards.back: The key: add a random suffix to spread the writes.

cards.front: In DynamoDB, repeated reads need microsecond latency with minimal code change. What do you add?
cards.back: DAX, the DynamoDB-compatible in-memory cache.

cards.front: DAX or ElastiCache: which one caches lists, sets and hashes for many data sources?
cards.back: ElastiCache.

cards.front: In DynamoDB, private subnets must reach a table without a NAT device. What do you add?
cards.back: A gateway endpoint for DynamoDB.

cards.front: In DynamoDB, which endpoint serves on-premises servers: gateway or interface?
cards.back: An interface endpoint (AWS PrivateLink).

cards.front: In DynamoDB, storage is most of a table's bill, and old items are rarely read. Which table class?
cards.back: DynamoDB Standard-IA.

cards.front: In DynamoDB, backups must survive deletion by an admin and exist in another account. What do you use?
cards.back: AWS Backup with Vault Lock and cross-account copies.

cards.front: In a DynamoDB global table with default settings, which write wins a conflict?
cards.back: The last writer wins.

cards.front: In DynamoDB, users may read only items whose partition key is their own ID. Which condition key?
cards.back: dynamodb:LeadingKeys.

cards.front: In DynamoDB, can one transaction write to tables in two Regions?
cards.back: No. One account and one Region only.

cards.front: In DynamoDB, can BatchWriteItem run UpdateItem requests?
cards.back: No. BatchWriteItem does not support UpdateItem requests.
